safetyNote: Poisonous: do not eat. Russula nobilis (also called R. mairei) can cause stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea after ingestion. Cooking does not make it a suitable food. Similar red brittlegills are difficult to identify from appearance alone. If ingestion is suspected and symptoms develop, contact a poison centre or medical service and keep a specimen for identification.

sections.title: Red cap and fragile gills
sections.text: The smooth cap is commonly 3–9 cm wide, rose-pink to bright red, sometimes unusually pale. It begins convex and generally remains rounded or only shallowly depressed as it matures; the margin is not prominently striate. Its surface is slightly sticky when wet but matt when dry. The cap skin can usually be peeled only about one third of the way toward the centre, exposing pink flesh beneath. The close, white to faintly cream gills are narrowly attached to the stem and crumble easily; a faint greenish sheen is possible.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and spore deposit
sections.text: The short white stem is smooth, firm and brittle, often a little club-shaped, without a ring or volva. The flesh is predominantly white and breaks rather than tearing into long fibres. A faint coconut-like smell may occur in young specimens, but is not reliable. The flesh is reported as very acrid; tasting a suspected poisonous mushroom is not an appropriate identification step. The spore deposit is white to off-white.

sections.title: Beech association and confusion
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species fruits on soil beneath beech trees, particularly in beech woodland, mainly from late summer through autumn in Europe. It can be confused with Russula emetica, another poisonous red brittlegill usually associated with conifers. R. emetica often develops a deeper central depression and its cap skin generally peels farther, but red Russula species overlap in appearance. Host tree, brittleness and cap characters must be considered together, and microscopy may still be needed.

sections.title: Poisoning and name
sections.text: Russula nobilis has also appeared in guides under the name Russula mairei. The German Society for Mycology lists that older name among fungi associated with gastrointestinal poisoning. The Woodland Trust and field mycology guides describe the beechwood sickener as toxic, causing abdominal symptoms, vomiting and diarrhoea. The exact irritant is not established in these sources. Avoid consumption rather than relying on cooking or the absence of a severe reaction in someone else.

traits: Smooth rose-pink to red cap, usually 3–9 cm; convex and only shallowly depressed when mature
Cap margin not distinctly striate; cap skin peels about one third toward the centre, revealing pink flesh
Crowded white, brittle gills narrowly attached to the stem, sometimes faintly greenish
Short firm white stem with chalk-like brittle flesh; no ring or volva
White to off-white spore deposit; young specimens may have a faint coconut-like odour
Ectomycorrhizal beneath beech, mainly late summer to autumn
